title: Netiquette Guidelines
summary: Provides a minimal set of guidelines for network etiquette that organizations may adapt for their own use. It covers manners for one-to-one communication such as mail and talk, and for one-to-many communication such as lists and news. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Good manners for the Internet: be polite and think before you post.

subtitle: A short, bulleted rulebook of good manners for email, mailing lists, Usenet and early Internet services.

tldr.problem: New users were joining an Internet that had been built by technically minded people, and they did not know its culture or its unwritten rules of behaviour.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a minimum set of guidelines in bulleted form, split into one-to-one communication, one-to-many communication and information services, with separate advice for users, administrators and moderators.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. Organizations are free to take the list and adapt it for their own use.

facts.label: Talk line length
facts.value: No more than 70 characters and 12 lines

today: RFC 1855 is an Informational memo from October 1995, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its advice describes the services of that time, such as Gopher, Wais and NetNews.

sections.title: Why Netiquette Was Written
sections.content:
RFC 1855 says that the Internet's early users had grown up with it and understood the transport and the protocols. By 1995 the community also included newbies, people who are new to the environment and do not need to know about protocols. The guide offers a minimum set of behaviours to bring them into the Internet culture quickly.

The text is deliberately written in a bulleted format so that an organization can adapt it and so that any one item is easy to find. It also warns individuals that whoever supplies their access, be it a provider, a university or an employer, has its own regulations about ownership of mail and files and about what is proper to post, so they should check with the local authority.
sections.eli5: When new kids join a club, someone should tell them how things are done there. This document is that short list of club manners for the Internet.

sections.title: One-to-One: Mail and Talk
sections.content:
One-to-one communication is a dialog, as if face-to-face. Common courtesy matters even more online, because body language and tone of voice must be inferred. The mail advice includes: unless you use encryption, assume mail is not secure and never put in it anything you would not put on a postcard; respect copyright; do not change the wording of a message you forward; never send chain letters; and do not send heated messages ("flames") even when provoked.

It also gives practical habits. Give the message a subject that reflects its content, include a short signature (a rule of thumb is no longer than 4 lines), use mixed case because UPPER CASE LOOKS AS IF YOU'RE SHOUTING, limit lines to fewer than 65 characters, and avoid sending a file larger than 50 Kilobytes. The RFC points out that the cost of an e-mail message is paid about equally by sender and recipient, which is a fundamental economic reason why unsolicited advertising is unwelcome.

For talk, an interactive two-person chat, it advises using no more than 70 characters per line and no more than 12 lines, saying goodbye before ending the session, and remembering that talk interrupts the other person. Administrators are told to have written guidelines for improper or forged traffic, to handle requests by the next business day, and to keep the "Postmaster" and "Root" aliases read by someone.
sections.eli5: Writing to one person is like a polite chat. Be kind, keep it short, do not shout, and wait to cool down before sending an angry note.

sections.title: One-to-Many: Lists and NetNews
sections.content:
Everything that applies to mail also applies when writing to many people, with the added risk of offending a great many more of them. The general advice is to read a mailing list or newsgroup for one to two months before posting, to remember that large audiences (possibly your next boss) will see your words and that lists are frequently archived, and to keep messages brief and on topic.

Be careful with replies, since a reply often goes back to the address of the whole list or group. Do not use delivery receipts or vacation programs on lists. Do not get involved in flame wars. If you ask a question, post a summary of the answers. Subscription messages should be saved because they usually explain how to unsubscribe.

NetNews is split into hierarchies such as sci, comp, news, rec, soc, talk, biz and alt. The guide explains cross-posting, reading a whole thread before replying, cancelling only your own articles, and marking movie or book discussions with "Spoilers". Administrators are asked to publish their archive and logging policies, and moderators to post the FAQ and charter regularly.
sections.eli5: Posting to a group is like speaking in a crowded room. Listen first, stay on topic, and do not hit "reply to all" by accident.

sections.title: Information Services
sections.content:
The third part covers services such as Gopher, Wais, the World Wide Web, ftp, telnet, MUDs, MOOs and IRC. The basic reminder is that all these services belong to someone else, and the people who pay the bills make the rules. Users should not assume that any information they find is up-to-date or accurate, and should remember that anything submitted without security technology travels over the Internet "in the clear".

Further user advice: use a nearby mirror server when one is listed, avoid "dumping" files on someone else's FTP site, and spread load by avoiding rush hour. For real-time services, listen first to learn the group's culture, do not greet people with automated client features, and respect a user's nickname or pseudonym.

Administrators are told to say clearly what may be copied, to keep READMEs current and in plain ascii text, to date time-sensitive material, to test with a variety of clients, and to tell users what they plan to do with any information they collect, such as web feedback.
sections.eli5: Websites and file servers belong to somebody. Treat them like someone else's house: follow the house rules and do not make a mess.

sections.title: Security and Status of the Memo
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document is the product of the Responsible Use of the Network (RUN) Working Group of the IETF and is published as FYI 28. Its status text states that it provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

The bibliography lists the books, FAQs and other works used to gather the material. Items not found in them came from the experience of the IETF-RUN Working Group.
sections.eli5: This is a list of advice, not a law. It does not try to teach computer security.
